clue.text: Believe councillor holds legal position

indicators.note: the abbreviation for councillor holds the other piece inside it, as if gripping it

parts.note: in football a player who is onside is in a legal position

explanation.surface: A councillor believes some legal post is held by them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legal position' reads as a job in law, but it is the football sense: ONSIDE, the opposite of offside.
explanation.definitionFit: To consider something so is to hold it as true, a synonym of believing it.

clue.text: Clubs throw minors out, looking embarrassed

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit

indicators.note: throw ... out together say the letters are thrown into disorder
out completes throw ... out, putting the letters out of their order

explanation.surface: Clubs eject under-age drinkers, who leave red-faced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw ... out' looks like a club ejecting under-age drinkers; the two words together are the anagram signal, giving RIMSON.
explanation.definitionFit: A crimson face is a deep red one, the colour of a blush of shame.

clue.text: Pinch attractive girl, do we see?

indicators.note: asks us to look at the light as written: read upward it shows a word that goes up

parts.note: an attractive girl in a poster is a pin-up: here the word pin set going up

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether pinching an attractive girl is what we witness.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down light, NIP read from the bottom gives PIN going up: PIN-UP, the attractive girl.
explanation.definitionFit: To nip is to squeeze sharply between finger and thumb, a synonym for pinch.

clue.text: Share admitted by dreadful liar making no sense

indicators.note: admitted by means let inside, so the share goes within the other piece
dreadful says the letters of liar are in a terrible mess

parts.note: a ration is a fixed share

explanation.surface: A terrible liar lets slip a share of the truth, talking nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadful' is the anagram signal, giving IRAL; 'admitted by' puts the share in the middle of that scramble.
explanation.definitionFit: Irrational means contrary to reason or logic, so it describes something without sense.

clue.text: Lift up old key

parts.note: ex means former or old, as in an ex-partner
Alt is a key on a computer keyboard

explanation.surface: Someone raises an old key from the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: To exalt is to raise someone high in rank or esteem.

clue.text: Churchman that, moving, must abandon his rank

definitions.meaning: a senior cleric in charge of a diocese

definitions.text: that, moving, must abandon his rank
definitions.meaning: the chess piece that moves only diagonally, so every move takes it off the row (rank) it stood on

explanation.surface: A clergyman who changes post has to give up his title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' looks like status in the church, but in chess a rank is a row of the board; the diagonal-moving piece always leaves its row.
explanation.definitionFit: A prelate overseeing a diocese, and the diagonal-moving chess piece named after that cleric.

clue.text: "I lead" in Russian

parts.note: the van is the leading part of an army, so to be in the van is to lead

explanation.surface: A Russian phrase book gives the translation of 'I lead'.
explanation.walkthrough: The quote marks dress 'I lead' as a phrase to translate; it is I plus VAN, the vanguard.
explanation.definitionFit: A common Russian man's first name, so it stands for a typical Russian.

clue.text: Put up easy catch: when you've gone, he comes in

definitions.text: when you've gone, he comes in

parts.note: to house someone is to put them up
in cricket a sitter is a very easy catch

explanation.surface: A fielder dollies up an easy catch, and the next batsman walks in.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket misleads: the incoming batsman is a red herring. A sitter is the easiest of catches.
explanation.definitionFit: This person minds a home while its owners are away, arriving as they leave.

clue.text: Excuse pressure to send message again

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
to retext is to send a text message once more

explanation.surface: Someone presses for an excuse to send a message a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretext is a false reason given to hide the real one.

clue.text: Better make certain one gets doctor round

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the doctor goes round, enclosing the other piece

parts.note: MD is a doctor of medicine
to prove something is to establish it for certain

explanation.surface: A patient is sure to get better once the doctor does a round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' here is the adjective, not the verb; 'gets' is only a link, and 'round' has the doctor enclosing the proof.
explanation.definitionFit: Improved, as an adjective, means made superior, a synonym of better.

clue.text: Caesar's decree found in the yard, for one

parts.note: an emperor's possession is imperial, and Caesar was the Roman emperor's title
a measure is a legislative act or decree

explanation.surface: An edict of the Roman emperor turned up in the courtyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The yard' looks like a courtyard where something was found; it is the unit of length, three feet.
explanation.definitionFit: The yard is a unit in the old British system of weights and lengths, so it is an example of one.

clue.text: Clothes blue? That's hardly novel

parts.note: shorts are clothes: short trousers
blue is the colour of the UK Conservative Party, so a Tory is a blue

explanation.surface: Blue clothes are nothing new, someone shrugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardly novel' sounds like 'not new', but it means not long enough to count as a novel. A Tory is a British Conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiction too brief to be a full-length book is something less than a novel.

clue.text: Getting dated, old boy only put on perfume

parts.note: OB stands for old boy, a former pupil
sole means only, as in sole survivor
scent is perfume

explanation.surface: An ageing old boy has only dabbed on some perfume.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsolescent describes something falling out of use, on its way to being out of date.

clue.text: Just in time, retreated a little

indicators.note: a little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone pulled back in the nick of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just in time' reads as one phrase; split it after 'Just', the definition, and 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mere and just both mean nothing more than, as in a mere child or just a child.

clue.text: Seize public land, we hear, and animals

explanation.walkthrough: COMMON said aloud gives COMMAN, joined to DEER.
explanation.definitionFit: To commandeer is to take possession of something, especially for military use.

clue.text: Performances cancelled? Just as well these stayed away

clue.text: In second court case, receiving new penalty

explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside ACTION after its A; 'In' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A sanction is a punishment imposed for breaking a rule.

clue.text: Girl toils to play as member of orchestra

parts.note: Vi is a short girl's name, from Violet

indicators.note: to play the letters is to set them in a new arrangement

explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' sounds musical in this surface, but it is the anagram signal: TOILS becomes OLIST.

clue.text: Criminal is sick — to no purpose?

explanation.definitionFit: A villain is a wrongdoer, a synonym for a criminal.

clue.text: Gave in — abandoned resistance to sour temper

explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' looks like giving up; it scrambles GAVE IN into VINEGA, then R.
explanation.definitionFit: Vinegar figuratively means sourness of temper or speech, from the acid liquid's sharp taste.

clue.text: In popular language, protest against credit being short

indicators.note: against means placed next to, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: a demo is a protest march

indicators.note: short means losing a last letter, so the word for credit is cut

parts.note: tick is British slang for credit, as in buying on tick

explanation.walkthrough: 'Being short' takes the last letter off TICK to give TIC. Buying 'on tick' is British for buying on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Demotic is the everyday vernacular of ordinary people, as against a formal or literary register.

clue.text: Bird one may find in wood
